description: A visitor's guide to the Red Fort (Lal Qila) in Delhi: built by Shah Jahan as the palace-fortress of Shahjahanabad, its role in 1857 and on Independence Day, what to see from Lahori Gate and Chhatta Chowk to the Diwan-i-Aam and Diwan-i-Khas, the museums, the Monday closure, tickets, the metro, and nearby Old Delhi.
dek: The Red Fort was the palace-fortress of the Mughal emperors in Delhi, and it is where India's Prime Minister raises the flag every Independence Day.

parent.label: UNESCO World Heritage Sites in India

intro: Shah Jahan moved the Mughal capital from Agra to Delhi and built a new city, Shahjahanabad, with the Red Fort as its palace-fortress. Construction ran from 1639 to 1648, in red sandstone walls around palaces of marble.

The fort was the seat of the Mughal emperors until 1857, when the last emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, was tried and exiled by the British, who then occupied it. Since 1947 the Prime Minister has addressed the nation from its ramparts on Independence Day. The Red Fort Complex, which includes the older Salimgarh Fort, was inscribed by UNESCO in 2007.
quickAnswer: The Red Fort (Lal Qila) in Old Delhi was built by Shah Jahan between 1639 and 1648 and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It is closed on Mondays and open on other days from morning to late afternoon; tickets are sold by the ASI, including online. The nearest metro station is Lal Qila on the Violet Line. Allow two to three hours, and combine it with Chandni Chowk and the Jama Masjid.
takeaways: Built by Shah Jahan between 1639 and 1648 as the palace of Shahjahanabad.
Closed on Mondays; check current hours with the ASI.
Enter through Lahori Gate and the covered Chhatta Chowk bazaar.
Lal Qila metro station (Violet Line) is closest; Chandni Chowk (Yellow Line) is a short walk.
Combine it with Chandni Chowk, the Jama Masjid and an Old Delhi heritage walk.

items.name: Lahori Gate and Chhatta Chowk
body: The main gate, facing Chandni Chowk, leads into a covered bazaar that still sells crafts and souvenirs.

items.name: Diwan-i-Aam
body: The Hall of Public Audience, with the emperor's marble throne canopy.

items.name: Diwan-i-Khas
body: The Hall of Private Audience in white marble, once home to the Peacock Throne, which was taken to Persia in 1739.

items.name: Rang Mahal and the palace pavilions
body: Marble pavilions linked by the Nahr-i-Bihisht, the 'stream of paradise' water channel.

items.name: Moti Masjid
body: A small marble mosque added by Aurangzeb.

items.name: Museums
body: Several museums inside the fort cover the Mughal period, the freedom struggle and 1857; check which galleries are open.

sections.heading: A short history
paras: After Nadir Shah's raid in 1739 and the decline of Mughal power, the fort remained the emperor's residence. Following the uprising of 1857, the British demolished many of its buildings and garrisoned it. It stayed a military cantonment for much of the 20th century, and the Indian Army handed it over for heritage use in 2003.

sections.heading: Visiting practicalities
list: Closed on Mondays; open other days from morning to late afternoon.
Tickets from the ASI, at counters or online; carry ID.
Security checks at the entrance; carry only a small bag.
A sound and light show has been held in the evenings; check current timings.
Allow two to three hours, more for the museums.

sections.heading: How to reach
list: Metro: Lal Qila station (Violet Line) is closest; Chandni Chowk (Yellow Line) is about a 15-minute walk.
By road: parking is limited; use the metro or a cab drop-off.
From New Delhi Railway Station: about 3 km.

items.name: Old Delhi
body: Chandni Chowk, the Jama Masjid, Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib and the old lanes.

links.label: Things to do in Old Delhi

items.name: Heritage walks
body: Guided walks through Shahjahanabad's bazaars and havelis.

sections.heading: A half-day in Old Delhi

rows: Red Fort, entering by Lahori Gate
Walk or ride a cycle-rickshaw down Chandni Chowk
Jama Masjid (outside prayer times), then the spice market at Khari Baoli

after: On Mondays, when the fort is closed, do Chandni Chowk and the Jama Masjid, and visit the fort another day.

safety: Timings, closures and ticket rules are set by the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) or the site authority and change from time to time; check the official website before you go, and buy tickets only on official portals.
Do not climb on or touch carvings, and follow the site's rules on photography, drones and tripods.
Weekends and holidays are crowded; arrive at opening time for the calmest visit.
Keep valuables secure in Chandni Chowk's crowded lanes.

faqs.q: Is the Red Fort open on Monday?
faqs.a: No. The Red Fort is closed on Mondays.
The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, between 1639 and 1648.

faqs.q: Which metro station is nearest to the Red Fort?
faqs.a: Lal Qila on the Violet Line; Chandni Chowk on the Yellow Line is also close.

faqs.q: How long does it take to see the Red Fort?
What happens at the Red Fort on Independence Day?
faqs.a: The Prime Minister raises the national flag and addresses the nation from the ramparts; the fort is closed to visitors around the day.

faqs.q: Is the Red Fort a UNESCO site?
faqs.a: Yes. The Red Fort Complex was inscribed in 2007.
